title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1LC1RD_1RA1LA_0RA0RE_0RC---_1RF0LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1LC1RD_1RA1LA_0RA0RE_0RC---_1RF0LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to an orbit. A step takes W A> 0 b^N 1 (b = 110) to W' A> 0 b^N' 1 with N' = (3N + c)/2, where the new wall W' and c are computed from the wall W and the parity of N. Lean proves the transfer loop behind the 3/2, the step map for every wall on which its simulator answers, and that, as long as it answers along the orbit, the machine halts from blank tape exactly when the orbit reaches a halting step. The map has been iterated for 40,000 steps without a halt (the plain-simulation map for 300,000), and no wall with a halting step has been found in a search of the wall graph: no halting mechanism is known for this machine, but no invariant excluding one is proved.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 44,753 cells have been visited and 32,396 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.047). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.494).

claims.title: The transfer loop
claims.text: At a junction L 1 b^(x+2) 111 F> b^(y+1) 1 (b = 110, any tape L, blank on the right) one sweep of 18y + 50 steps gives L 1 b^x 111 F> b^(y+4) 1; by induction t sweeps move 2t copies out of the left block and 3t into the right one.

claims.title: The start of a step
claims.text: From the wall 1, 1 A> 0 b^(n+6) 1 reaches the first junction in 5n + 66 steps.

claims.title: The step map for every wall
claims.text: A step from W A> 0 b^N 1 has three parts: the head crosses the block and builds the junction L 1 b^x 111 F> b^(y+1) 1 with x = N − const; the transfer loop makes x mod 2, y + 3⌊x/2⌋ of it; the end of the step works on the wall and leaves W' A> 0 b^N' 1. The first and third parts are computed by a simulator that steps cell by cell near the wall and near the right end and crosses the middle of the long block only whole, by three shift rules; it never looks at the number of copies it crosses. Lean proves that whatever it answers is what the machine does: if stepMap (W, N) = (W', N') the machine goes from the first step start to the second, and if it answers halt the machine halts in that step. For every wall W and every N for which the simulator answers; it may answer stuck (N too small for the working room (about two copies of b per wall cell), a meeting with the block that the three rules do not cover, or out of fuel), which has not been seen along the orbit.

claims.title: Reduction to the orbit
claims.text: The run from blank tape reaches the step start 11101101111101 A> 0 b^48 1 after 10,206 steps. Let orbit be the orbit of the step map from there. If the map never answers stuck along the orbit, the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit reaches a halting step. Without any hypothesis: a halting step in the orbit gives a halt, and an orbit that goes on for ever gives a run that never halts.

claims.title: The first 40 steps of the orbit
claims.text: Lean's kernel evaluates the step map along the orbit: it answers with a next step for each of the first 40 steps (no halt, never stuck); after five steps the wall is 1 and N = 468 (step 1,133,743 of the run).

claims.title: The Lean step map agrees with plain simulation
claims.text: py/zonemap.py is the same simulator in Python. Along the orbit from 1 A> 0 b^468 1 it gives the same (W', N') as the plain step map of py/stepmap.py (one step simulated in C, three values of N per case) for 4,000 steps, when N has 2,349 bits and walls have up to 563 cells.

claims.title: Orbit of the Lean step map: 40,000 steps, never stuck
claims.text: From the step start at step 10,206 of the run the map answers with a next step 40,000 times in a row (no halt, never stuck); N then has 23,405 bits and 83 walls have occurred. A breadth-first search of all walls of at most 300 cells reachable from 1 with either parity of N (279 walls, 558 steps) finds no halting step and no stuck one.

claims.title: The step map by plain simulation
claims.text: A step goes from W A> 0 b^N 1 to W' A> 0 b^N' 1 with N' = (3N + c)/2 and (W', c) depending only on (W, N mod 2), checked on three values of N per case (py/stepmap.py, one step simulated by c/stepc.c). It agrees with the machine for the first ten steps after step 1,133,743 of the run (to step 4.1·109).

claims.title: 300,000 steps, no halt
claims.text: From 1 A> 0 b^468 1 (step 1,133,743 of the run) the map runs 300,000 steps without a halt; N then has about 175,000 bits; 117 walls occur, the wall 1 in 24% of the steps.

claims.title: No halting wall found
claims.text: Breadth-first search of the walls reachable from 1 with either parity (100 walls): no step halts. The halt needs A> 0 111 (A writes 1, B and D read the next two 1s, E reads a third); none of the tested steps with small N (3 to 39, the first 80 walls) gets there either.

claims.title: Why it may never halt
claims.text: The numbers in the wall grow like N only along runs of odd N and are absorbed into N by two even steps in a row, so the wall stays short; a halting configuration would need a wall shape the map has not produced in any explored branch. This is evidence, not an argument.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. By the reduction it halts iff the orbit of the step map reaches a halting step (given that the map keeps answering). No halting step is known at all; a proof of non-halting would need a description of every reachable wall (a tower of 3/2-counters) and of the steps on it.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine moves a block of N copies of 110 across a junction two in, three out, so N grows by 3/2 each step, while a wall on the left keeps a tower of smaller counters driven by the parity of N. No halting wall has been found.

facts.text: The sweep loop, for any wall and any length, proved in Lean.
Of the step map from the run: no halt, N has 175,000 bits.
Searched with either parity: no halting step.

sections.heading: A block moved two in, three out
html: Write b for the three cells 110. At the start of every step the tape is W A> 0 bN 1: a short wall W on the left, then one long block of N copies of b. The head builds a junction 111 and sweeps: each sweep runs right to the end of the tape and back, takes two copies of b from the block on the left of the junction and adds three to the block on its right. When the left block is used up, the right block has about 3N/2 copies, and the next step starts. The tape grows on the right at each sweep (the square-root side); the wall on the left changes only once per step and grows slowly (the logarithmic side).
The parity of N decides how the step ends. The wall is a stack of counters:

wall WN evenN odd
11, 3N/2 + 71^4 b 1, (3N+9)/2
1^(3j+1) b 1 (j odd)1^(3j+4), 3N/2 + 71 b^(j+1) 1^3 b 1, (3N+9)/2
1^(3j+1) (j even)1, 3N/2 + 7 + j1^(3j+4) b 1, (3N+9)/2
1 b^k 1^3 b 11 b^k 1^6, 3N/2 + 7k even: 1 b^(3k/2+2) 1^3 b 1; k odd: 1^4 b 1 b^((3k-1)/2) 1^3 b 1
1 b^k 1^6k even: 1, 3N/2 + 3k/2 + 9; k odd: 1^4 b 1, 3N/2 + (3k+13)/2k even: 1^4 b 1; k odd: 1 (k is added into N)

So a run of alternating parities lengthens the wall 1^(3j+1); an odd step at the wrong moment turns it into a number k in the wall, and that number is itself multiplied by 3/2 at later odd steps, possibly spawning a further level. Two even steps fold the wall back into N. From the run: N = 468, 709, 1068, 1609, 2418, 3634, 5462, … with walls 1, 1, 1^4 b 1, 1^7, 1^10 b 1, 1^13, 1, …

sections.heading: The step map, for every wall at once
html: There are infinitely many walls, and the end of a step looks different for each. What they share: the head crosses the middle of the long block of b's only whole, in one of three ways:

So the parts of a step before and after the transfer loop can be computed by a small simulator that steps cell by cell near the wall and near the right end (keeping some copies of b on each side as working room) and jumps over the copies between by a shift rule. It never looks at how many copies it jumps. Lean proves that whatever this simulator answers is what the machine does (lean/Zone.lean, generic; lean/Reduction.lean, this machine), and chains it with the transfer loop into a computable step map stepMap (W, N) = (W', N'), halt, or stuck (no answer).

The theorem halts_iff: if the map never answers stuck along the orbit that starts at step 10,206 of the run (11101101111101 A> 0 b^48 1), the machine halts from blank tape exactly when that orbit reaches a halting step. The kernel checks the first 40 steps; the same simulator in Python has run 40,000 steps (always answering) and agrees with plain simulation for 4,000.
What is still missing for a statement with no hypothesis is a proof that the simulator never gets stuck; and for a decision, a description of all reachable walls.

sections.heading: No way to halt has been seen
html: The machine halts only when E reads a 1, which needs the head in A on a 0 followed by 111. In the 300,000 steps of the map from the run, and in every step from the 100 walls reachable with arbitrary parities, this never happens. Unlike the Antihydra-type cryptids, no halting condition on the map is known; but the reachable walls form a tower of counters with no proved description, so non-halting is not proved either.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.047). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.494).
After 109 steps the tape spans 44,753 cells (21 left of the start, 32,221 right), with a density of 1s of 0.724.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A block of N copies of 110 is moved across a junction two copies in, three out (N -> (3N+c)/2); the parity of N rewrites a 'wall' on the left that holds a tower of smaller 3/2-counters. Lean proves the step map for every wall (computed by a simulator that never looks at N) and the reduction to its orbit; no step that halts has been found.
